To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Shc adaptor is essential for NT4-dependent neuronal survival in vivo, but not for BDNF-dependent neuronal survival or for neuronal differentiation.
the Shc binding domain in the TrkB receptor is essential for the neurotrophic actions of NT4 in vivo but is dispensable for the survival and differentiation responses of BDNF in vivo.
the Shc adaptor binding domain in the TrkB receptor is required for the survival of NT4-dependent sensory but not for the survival of BDNF-dependent sensory neurons in the mouse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which neurotrophins regulate neuronal development and function.
the role of neurotrophins and their receptors during development of the nervous system and the mechanisms by which neurotrophin signaling controls the survival and differentiation processes.
the molecular and genetic basis of neurotrophic factor function in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Shc adaptor protein is not required for the diverse responses to BDNFS and NT4S, including neuronal differentiation.

a single mutation in the Shc binding domain of trkB results in a loss of NT4-dependent neurons and a reduction in BDNF responses in vitro, but has only a modest effect on diverse in vivo responses to BDNFs.
a point mutation in the Shc binding motif of TrkB causes loss of NT4-dependent neurons without major effects on diverse BDNF responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BDNF/NT4-dependent survival of peripheral and central sensory neurons requires the intact Shc binding site of TrkB.
NT4-dependent neurons in vivo are more sensitive to the loss of the Shc binding domain than are BDNF-dependent cells.
the Shc binding region in the intracellular domain of TrkB is required for NT4 but not for BDNF signaling in vivo.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neurotrophin receptor TrkB mediates distinct responses to its two ligands, BDNF and neurotrophins-4, which are differentially regulated by the intracellular signaling pathway.
the Ras/MAP kinase pathway is not required for BDNF- or NT4-dependent differentiation of CNS and sensory neurons.
BDNF and/or NT4 signaling through TrkB are required for the survival of many, if not most, sensory neurons in the mouse, but are not necessary for the differentiation or function of these neurons.
